He has literary pretensions and a drawer full of drafts.
Her writing is honest and free of pretension.

entries.meaning: A false reason given to hide the real one. ---
examples: The search was a pretext to look for something else.
He left on the pretext of an urgent phone call.
Both pretexts fell apart under questioning.

entries.meaning: A crisp or soft baked snack made of dough twisted into a knot. ---
examples: He bought a soft pretzel from a street cart.
The bar puts out bowls of pretzels.
She twisted the dough into a pretzel and salted it.

entries.meaning: How widespread something is within a population. ---
examples: The prevalence of diabetes has risen steadily.
Researchers tracked the prevalence of the virus by county.
The prevalence of cheating surprised the faculty.

entries.meaning: The setting of prices, or the prices themselves. ---
examples: Their pricing is higher than the competition.
The company changed its pricing in January.
Pricing for the new plan starts at ten dollars a month.

entries.meaning: The position of being a priest, or priests taken as a group. ---
examples: He entered the priesthood at twenty-six.
The priesthood has been shrinking for decades.
She writes about women and the priesthood.

entries.meaning: A low-growing plant with pale yellow or brightly colored spring flowers. ---
examples: Primroses came up along the fence in March.
She planted a primrose in the window box.
The woods were full of wild primroses.

entries.meaning: The daughter of a king or queen, or the wife of a prince. ---
examples: The princess waved from the balcony.
Both princesses attended the ceremony.
She dressed as a princess for Halloween.

entries.meaning: Something treated as more important than other things. ---
examples: Safety is our top priority.
Let's agree on three priorities for the quarter.
Sleep became a priority after the diagnosis.

entries.meaning: A special advantage given to one person or group, or the general state of having such advantages. ---
examples: Driving is a privilege, not a right.
The course examines race and privilege in America.
The inmates lost their visiting privileges.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A professional, especially in sport, or an argument in favor of something. ---
examples: He's a pro at fixing old engines.
We listed the pros and cons on a napkin.
Two touring pros ran the clinic.

entries.meaning: How likely something is to happen, or the branch of mathematics that measures it. ---
examples: There is a high probability of rain tonight.
The class covers probability and statistics.
The model assigns probabilities to each outcome.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: The legal process of proving a will and settling a dead person's estate. ---
examples: The house is still in probate.
Probate can drag on for more than a year.
She filed the will with the probate court.

entries.meaning: A live bacterium taken as a supplement or in food to help digestion. ---
examples: The doctor suggested a probiotic after the antibiotics.
Yogurt with live cultures contains probiotics.
She takes a daily probiotic with breakfast.

entries.meaning: A situation that causes trouble, or a question to be solved. ---
examples: We have a problem with the heating.
Do the odd-numbered problems for homework.
That's not a problem I can fix today.

entries.meaning: A formal action or event, especially a legal one. ---
examples: The court proceedings lasted three weeks.
He was barred from the proceedings.
A disciplinary proceeding was opened against the officer.
entries.contrast: Usually used in the plural: legal proceedings, divorce proceedings.

entries.meaning: The treating of raw material or information to turn it into something usable. ---
examples: Meat processing employs most of the town.
Your refund is still in processing.
Data processing used to be its own department.

entries.meaning: A person who watches students during an exam to prevent cheating. ---
examples: The proctor collected everyone's phones.
Two proctors walked the aisles the whole time.
Ask the proctor if you need more paper.

entries.meaning: A young person with a remarkable natural talent. ---
examples: She was a chess prodigy at eight.
The conservatory is full of prodigies.
Not every prodigy becomes a great adult artist.

entries.meaning: Rude or offensive language, or a single word of that kind. ---
examples: The coach was ejected for shouting profanity.
He muttered a string of profanities.
The broadcast bleeps out any profanity.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: Someone who does a job that requires training and qualifications, or who does it for pay. ---
examples: Hire a professional to check the wiring.
The conference is aimed at young professionals.
As a professional, she never discusses her clients.

entries.meaning: A good level of skill or ability in something. ---
examples: The job requires proficiency in Spanish.
He tested at intermediate proficiency.
Proficiency comes from practice, not talent.

entries.meaning: The practice of judging or selecting people based on typical characteristics of a group. ---
examples: The lawsuit accuses the department of racial profiling.
Criminal profiling is far less exact than television suggests.
Customer profiling drives the ads you see.

entries.meaning: A hormone that prepares the body for pregnancy. ---
examples: Her progesterone levels came back low.
The pill combines estrogen and progesterone.
Progesterone rises in the second half of the cycle.

entries.meaning: The writing of computer code, or the shows a channel schedules. ---
examples: He teaches programming to high schoolers.
The network changed its evening programming.
Programming for kids fills the Saturday morning slot.

entries.meaning: A gradual movement forward through a series of stages. ---
examples: The drug slows the progression of the disease.
The song uses a simple chord progression.
Her career followed a steady progression.

entries.meaning: Someone who supports social reform and change in politics. ---
examples: Progressives pushed hard for the amendment.
She ran as a progressive and won the primary.
The party's progressives voted against the compromise.

entries.meaning: An official order forbidding something. ---
examples: The city lifted its prohibition on backyard chickens.
There is a prohibition against gifts from vendors.
Both prohibitions expired last year.
entries.contrast: The h is silent in American speech: proh-uh-BISH-un, not proh-hib-.

entries.meaning: An object thrown or fired through the air. ---
examples: The blast turned the glass into projectiles.
Police recovered the projectile from the wall.
Any loose tool becomes a projectile in a crash.

entries.meaning: The state of being important and widely known. ---
examples: The case rose to prominence after the documentary.
She gained prominence as a civil rights lawyer.
The issue has lost prominence since the election.

entries.meaning: A statement that you will certainly do something. ---
examples: He made a promise he couldn't keep.
She kept her promise to call every Sunday.
Campaign promises are easy to make and hard to fund.

entries.meaning: Someone who organizes and publicizes events, or who actively supports a cause. ---
examples: The concert promoter canceled two dates.
Promoters are expecting a sellout crowd.
He is a tireless promoter of local business.

entries.meaning: One of the pointed parts of a fork, plug, or similar object. ---
examples: One prong of the fork was bent.
The plug has three prongs.
The second prong of the strategy is cutting costs.

entries.meaning: An offer or suggestion, or a statement that can be judged true or false. ---
examples: He made me an interesting business proposition.
The ballot proposition failed by a wide margin.
Running a restaurant is a risky proposition.

entries.meaning: Correct or socially acceptable behavior. ---
examples: The judge questioned the propriety of the meeting.
She has a strong sense of propriety.
Nobody doubted the propriety of his motives.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with property; propriety is about correct behavior.

entries.meaning: The force that pushes a vehicle forward. ---
examples: The lab works on electric propulsion for satellites.
Jet propulsion changed air travel completely.
The submarine uses nuclear propulsion.

entries.meaning: Ordinary written language, as opposed to poetry. ---
examples: Her prose is plain and fast-moving.
He writes both poetry and prose.
The essay is a fine piece of prose.

entries.meaning: Someone who searches an area for gold, oil, or other valuable minerals. ---
examples: Prospectors flooded California in 1849.
An old prospector filed the original claim.
The prospector panned that creek all summer.

entries.meaning: A printed document describing an investment, a school, or a planned project. ---
examples: Read the prospectus before you buy the fund.
The college mailed us a glossy prospectus.
Both prospectuses leave out the fees.

entries.meaning: The state of being successful and financially comfortable. ---
examples: The postwar years brought broad prosperity.
The town's prosperity depended on the mill.
They wished the couple health and prosperity.

entries.meaning: Artificial body parts, or the field that designs and fits them. ---
examples: Advances in prosthetics over the last decade have been remarkable.
The actor wore facial prosthetics for the role.
She studied prosthetics and orthotics in Chicago.

entries.meaning: A person who has sex for money. ---
examples: The film follows a prostitute in 1970s New York.
Police arrested two prostitutes and a client.
She played a prostitute in her first film role.

entries.meaning: The practice of having sex for money. ---
examples: Prostitution is legal in parts of Nevada.
The charge was reduced from prostitution to loitering.
The report studies why women enter prostitution.

entries.meaning: A country or region controlled and defended by a stronger state. ---
examples: The island was a British protectorate until 1968.
Several African protectorates gained independence in the 1960s.
The treaty turned the small kingdom into a French protectorate.

entries.meaning: A young person who is taught and helped along by someone older and more experienced. ---
examples: The senator hired his old protege as chief of staff.
She was a protege of the orchestra's former conductor.
Both proteges now run companies of their own.
entries.contrast: Usually written with accents — protégé. The last syllable rhymes with 'day'.

entries.meaning: An official set of rules for how something must be done. ---
examples: The hospital has a strict protocol for handling infections.
Emergency protocols were rewritten after the fire.
Sending that email broke every protocol in the office.

entries.meaning: A part that sticks out from a surface. ---
examples: A small bony protrusion on his heel made walking painful.
The old wall had odd protrusions every few feet.
The MRI showed a disc protrusion in her lower back.

entries.meaning: The care and protection that God or fate is believed to provide. ---
examples: She credited her survival to divine providence.
His letters keep returning to providence and the fate of the country.
They took the sudden rain as an act of providence.

entries.meaning: One of the large areas a country is divided into for government. ---
examples: Ontario is the most populous province in Canada.
Several northern provinces were hit by flooding.
He grew up in a rural province far from the capital.

entries.meaning: An action meant to make someone angry or to force a reaction. ---
examples: The dog bit him without any provocation.
Border provocations continued all week.
The speech was widely read as a deliberate provocation.

entries.meaning: A senior university official in charge of academic affairs. ---
examples: The provost announced a hiring freeze for next year.
She served as provost before becoming president of the college.
Both provosts signed the joint statement.

entries.meaning: Someone who moves quietly around a place at night, usually meaning to steal or do harm. ---
examples: A neighbor called the police about a prowler in the alley.
The dog barks at every prowler on the block.
Two prowlers showed up on the security camera.

entries.meaning: Nearness in space or time. ---
examples: We bought the house for its proximity to good schools.
The proximity of the two deadlines makes planning hard.
Sensors detect the proximity of another car.

entries.meaning: A person or thing that acts or stands in for another. ---
examples: She voted by proxy because she was out of the country.
The company routes its traffic through several proxies.
Test scores are a poor proxy for intelligence.

entries.meaning: Someone who is easily shocked by sex or rude language. ---
examples: Don't be such a prude — it's just a joke.
The movie was tame enough that even the prudes in the audience laughed.
He's no prude, but that scene made him uncomfortable.

entries.meaning: Careful good judgment that avoids unnecessary risk. ---
examples: Financial prudence carried the city through the recession.
There is a difference between fear and prudence.
Basic prudence says you should read the contract first.

entries.meaning: A false name used by a writer in place of a real one. ---
examples: She published her first novel under a pseudonym.
The letters were signed with an obvious pseudonym.
Several of his pseudonyms came to light only after his death.
entries.contrast: The p is silent: 'SOO-duh-nim'.

entries.meaning: A skin disease that produces dry red patches covered with silvery scales. ---
examples: Cold weather makes his psoriasis worse.
She sees a dermatologist for psoriasis twice a year.
The new cream cleared up the psoriasis on his elbows.
entries.contrast: The p is silent and the stress falls on the second syllable: 'suh-RY-uh-sis'.

entries.meaning: The human mind, especially its deeper feelings and attitudes. ---
examples: The attack left a scar on the national psyche.
He writes about the psyche of the American voter.
Losing that game damaged the whole team's psyche.
entries.contrast: The final e is pronounced: 'SY-kee', not 'syke'.

entries.meaning: The branch of medicine that deals with mental illness. ---
examples: She left surgery to study psychiatry.
Psychiatry has changed a great deal in fifty years.
He teaches psychiatry at the medical school.

entries.meaning: A person who claims to know things by supernatural means. ---
examples: Her aunt pays a psychic to read her cards every month.
Two psychics offered to help find the missing dog.
The psychic told him he would travel soon.

entries.meaning: Someone whose job is to get public attention for a client. ---
examples: The actor's publicist released a short statement.
She works as a publicist for a small record label.
Both publicists denied the rumor.

entries.meaning: A village of flat-roofed adobe houses built by Native peoples of the American Southwest. ---
examples: We toured an ancient pueblo outside Santa Fe.
The pueblos of New Mexico draw visitors all year.
Wooden ladders connect the upper levels of the pueblo.

entries.meaning: A short blast of air, smoke, or breath. ---
examples: A puff of smoke came out of the engine.
He took two quick puffs on his inhaler.
The wind arrived in warm puffs all afternoon.

entries.meaning: An act of using force to move something toward you, or the force itself. ---
examples: Give the cord a firm pull to start the mower.
You can feel the pull of the current out here.
A couple of hard pulls got the drawer open.

entries.meaning: A collapsed star that sends out regular pulses of radio waves. ---
examples: The telescope picked up signals from a distant pulsar.
Some pulsars spin hundreds of times a second.
A graduate student found the first pulsar in 1967.

entries.meaning: A light gray volcanic rock full of tiny holes, used for scrubbing skin. ---
examples: She keeps a block of pumice by the tub.
Pumice is light enough to float on water.
Rub the callus gently with pumice.

entries.meaning: A small hole made by a sharp object. ---
examples: A nail left a puncture in the rear tire.
The doctor cleaned the puncture on his palm.
Two punctures in the air mattress kept us up all night.

entries.meaning: A loud, rough style of rock music, or a young person who follows it. ---
examples: He grew up listening to punk and metal.
A couple of punks with green hair walked past.
The band's early records are pure punk.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A kick made by dropping the football and kicking it before it hits the ground. ---
examples: His punt pinned the other team at the five-yard line.
The offense stalled and had to settle for a punt.
Three of his punts traveled over fifty yards.

entries.meaning: The football player whose job is to punt the ball. ---
examples: The punter jogged out with the special teams unit.
Their punter was the best in the league last season.
Both punters struggled in the wind.

entries.meaning: The art of making puppets and performing with them. ---
examples: The museum has an exhibit on Indonesian puppetry.
She studied puppetry before going into animation.
The show combines live actors with puppetry.

entries.meaning: Food that has been blended into a thick, smooth paste. ---
examples: Stir a spoonful of tomato puree into the sauce.
The baby eats carrot puree twice a day.
The chef served scallops over two bright green purees.
entries.contrast: Usually written purée; the stress falls on the last syllable.

entries.meaning: The sudden removal of many people from an organization. ---
examples: The new director began a purge of senior staff.
Thousands disappeared during the party purges.
A purge of old files freed up half the server.

entries.meaning: The process of removing dirt or harmful substances from something. ---
examples: The village needs a simple water purification system.
Air purification helps a lot during allergy season.
The ritual is meant as a kind of spiritual purification.

entries.meaning: Someone who insists that traditional rules or methods be followed exactly. ---
examples: Purists say the remake ruined the story.
As a purist, he refuses to put ice in good whiskey.
Grammar purists still object to that usage.

entries.meaning: A person with very strict moral standards, especially about pleasure. ---
examples: Her grandfather was a puritan about money and drink.
The columnists called the new mayor a puritan.
Only a puritan would object to a glass of wine at lunch.

entries.meaning: The act of chasing someone, or of trying to achieve something. ---
examples: The chase ended after a ten-mile pursuit on the freeway.
She gave up a good salary in pursuit of a degree.
Hiking and photography are his favorite weekend pursuits.

entries.meaning: A person or business that supplies goods, especially food. ---
examples: The shop calls itself a purveyor of fine cheeses.
Local purveyors supply the restaurant with produce.
He became a purveyor of cheap rumors and worse advice.

entries.meaning: The thick yellowish liquid that forms in an infected wound. ---
examples: There was pus around the stitches.
If you see pus, call the doctor.
The dentist drained the pus from the abscess.

entries.meaning: An act of pressing something away from you, or an organized effort to achieve something. ---
examples: One hard push and the door swung open.
The company is making a push into the Asian market.
A few gentle pushes got the swing going.

entries.meaning: Someone who sells illegal drugs. ---
examples: The police arrested a pusher outside the school.
The film follows a small-time pusher in Baltimore.
Street pushers rarely know where the drugs come from.

entries.meaning: Someone who is easy to persuade or easy to defeat. ---
examples: Don't think she's a pushover just because she's polite.
That team is no pushover at home.
New teachers often get treated like pushovers.

entries.meaning: An exercise in which you lie face down and push your body up with your arms. ---
examples: He does fifty pushups every morning.
I can barely manage one pushup.
The coach made us do pushups after every mistake.
entries.contrast: Often written push-up with a hyphen; both spellings are common in the US.

entries.meaning: A gentle golf stroke that rolls the ball along the green toward the hole. ---
examples: He missed a three-foot putt on the last hole.
Her putts were falling all afternoon.
One good putt saved his round.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with cut, not with the verb put.

entries.meaning: The golf club used for rolling the ball along the green. ---
examples: He bought a new putter over the winter.
She lined up the shot with her putter.
The old putters in his bag are worth a fortune.

entries.meaning: A tall metal tower carrying power lines, or a marker cone used on a field or course. ---
examples: A row of pylons crosses the valley.
The ball landed just outside the orange pylon.
Ice brought down two pylons near the highway.

entries.meaning: A large pile of wood on which a dead body is burned. ---
examples: The village built a funeral pyre by the river.
Smoke from the pyres hung over the valley for days.
In the poem the hero is laid on a pyre.

entries.meaning: A shiny yellow mineral often mistaken for gold. ---
examples: The rock they brought back was only pyrite.
Pyrite is sometimes called fool's gold.
Tiny cubes of pyrite glittered in the shale.

entries.meaning: A display of fireworks, or the art of making and setting them off.
examples: The concert ended with pyrotechnics over the stadium.
A separate crew handles the pyrotechnics on tour.
The show's pyrotechnics set off the smoke alarms.
